Weiner claims that the memoir is an elaborate sleight of hand and speculates that Said decided to "spin" the story of his past--by telling the truth about it--when he heard about Weiner's inquiries. In the weeks since his essay appeared, Weiner's motives, methods, and assertions have been roundly attacked by Said and his friends, and Weiner has made some attempt at clarification. (Click for a recap of the controversy and links to relevant articles, or click here for my review of Out of Place .) 

         Just who is Edward Said that his family's real estate holdings and his grammar school records rate 7,000 words in Commentary , not to mention three years of research by a scholar in residence at the Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs? Followers of Middle East politics, as well as viewers of the NewsHour With Jim Lehrer , where Said often appears, know him as an eloquent spokesman for the Palestinian cause. Readers of The Nation know him as a formidable reviewer of opera and classical music. Several generations of graduate students in a number of disciplines know him as the author of Orientalism . The 30,000 literary scholars who make up the membership of the Modern Language Association--minus one who resigned in protest earlier this year over Said's election--know him as Mr. President. Readers of Al-Hayat , a London-based Arabic-language newspaper, and Al-Ahram , a Cairo weekly, know him as a regular commentator on politics and culture. Each of these identities--political activist, literary scholar, university professor, public intellectual--are, in Said's case, inordinately complex in and of themselves. The tensions between them--between intellectual, aesthetic, and political impulses that are felt with enormous passion and expressed with great vehemence--make Said an uncommonly interesting, and endlessly controversial, intellectual figure. 

         Most controversial--and most misunderstood--has been Said's involvement in Palestinian affairs. He has published half a dozen books on the plight of the Palestinians, including The Question of Palestine (1979), After the Last Sky (1986), and Peace and Its Discontents (1995), a scathing critique of the Oslo peace accords, which Said calls "the Palestinian Versailles." These writings, his relationship with PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat, and his many years of service in the Palestine National Council (the now-defunct Palestinian parliament in exile, from which he resigned in 1991 after being diagnosed with leukemia) have invited smears and misrepresentations: A decade ago Commentary branded him "The Professor of Terror." New York magazine once called him "Arafat's man in New York." And he showed up last spring, unnamed, in The                 New Yorker 's special "Money" issue as a well-dressed Columbia don rumored to be "on the payroll of the PLO." 

         Until very recently, Said has been an insistent voice for Palestinian statehood: He helped to draft the PLO's "Algiers Declaration" of 1988, which linked this aspiration to the recognition of Israel's right to exist. Over the years, he has often said that his own place in such a state would be as its toughest critic. Even as he has been unsparing in his indictments of Israeli and American policy, he has not let Arab governments--or the Palestinian leadership--off the hook. He has assailed the corrupt, authoritarian regimes that rule most of the Arab world, punctured the ideological phantasms of Pan-Arabist nationalism and reactionary Islam alike, and bemoaned the impoverished state of Arab cultural and intellectual life. He has also, within the Palestinian camp, been a consistent advocate of reconciliation with Israel and an opponent of terrorism. The Question of Palestine called for a "two-state solution" at a time when the official PLO ambition was total control over British Mandatory Palestine. The book, published in Israel in 1981, had, as of the mid-'90s, never been translated into Arabic or published in any Arab country. 

         In 1978, in the wake of the Camp David accords, Said delivered a message from Secretary of State Cyrus Vance to one of Arafat's top aides indicating that the United States would recognize the PLO as a legitimate party to peace talks in exchange for recognition of Israel. Arafat ignored the message. Fifteen years later, when Arafat and Israeli Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin shook hands on the White House lawn, Said, who had been invited to the event by its patron, Bill Clinton, stayed home. Since then, as bien-pensant American opinion has embraced the "peace process," Said has bemoaned Arafat's "capitulation" and grown increasingly disgusted with the chairman's dictatorial rule over a few scraps of occupied territory and with Israel's continued expropriation of Palestinian lands. In the New York Times Magazine last spring, he wrote that the Palestinian state toward which the peace process seemed, however pokily, to be tending could not provide democracy and justice for the Palestinians. Instead, he called for a single, "bi-national" state based on a constitution (something neither Israel nor the areas controlled by the Palestinian Authority currently has), with "the idea and practice of citizenship, not of ethnic or racial community, as the main vehicle for coexistence." 

         But to treat Said solely, or even primarily, as a political figure is necessarily to produce a distorted view of his life. He is, first and foremost, a literary critic, who wrote his Ph.D. at Harvard--on Joseph Conrad, a lifelong obsession--under Harry Levin, one of the champions of a comparative approach to literary study. Said's subsequent work has retained much of the expansive spirit and rigorous methodology of Levin's teachings. Beginnings: Intention and Method , the book which made Said's academic reputation, is a bulky study of how novels begin, carried out through painstakingly close formal analysis and displaying crushing erudition. 

         But Said's fame outside the American academy rests on Orientalism , his sweeping account of how Western art, literature, and scholarship have produced a deformed, biased picture of Arab and Muslim culture in the service of colonial domination. The impact of Orientalism far exceeded its subject, vast though that was. In addition to laying the groundwork for "post-colonial" studies as an area of inquiry, the book inspired a flurry of scholarship devoted to "the other"--to groups of people who, by virtue of race, gender, sexuality, or geographical location, are unable to represent themselves and so (to echo the line from Karl Marx that serves as the book's epigraph) "must be represented" by those more powerful. And Orientalism , with its harsh critiques of European philology and American social science, contributed to an epistemological shift in the American academy: Traditional disciplines were no longer to be taken for granted as the vehicles of objective knowledge but themselves became the objects of ideological analysis. 

         Both Said's methods and his substantive claims have come under attack. Because his theoretical debt to Michel Foucault and his unabashedly political intentions marked him as an avatar of the emerging academic left, a lot of the criticism came from traditional scholars. In the New York Review of Books , for example, the Princeton historian Bernard Lewis, one of the chief modern villains of Orientalism , decried Said's inflammatory tone and questioned his knowledge of history, philology, and Arabic. In a book called In Theory --a wholesale slaughter of the sacred cows of the postmodern Western intelligentsia--the Indian Marxist literary critic Aijaz Ahmad raised further questions about Said's mastery of his sources and accused him of self-aggrandizement and insufficient political discipline. Whereas Lewis attacks Said for trashing the norms and values of traditional scholarship, Ahmad rebukes him for hewing too closely to them. And while Lewis believes Said to be motivated by a crude anti-Western leftist animus, Ahmad finds him altogether too enamored of the canons of European literature and avers that Said possesses "a very conservative mind, essentially Tory in its structure." 

         Lewis and Ahmad are both right. Orientalism and its even more ambitious sequel Culture and Imperialism are works of passionate, almost agonized ambivalence. To read them is to encounter a mind at war with itself and the world (and ready to go to war with his critics, as any number of exchanges over the past quarter-century will show). His desire to use literary criticism as a weapon on the side of the oppressed sits athwart the pleasure he takes in letting his mind play over the meaning in a novel or a poem. The results are books at once exhausting in their detail and maddening in their omissions, uneven in tone, overreaching and underargued. "He is easily distracted" the critic John Leonard remarked in an appreciative review of Culture and Imperialism , "answering too many fire alarms, sometimes to pour on more petrol."

1. Central Critiques by Authorities
   - Princeton historian Bernard Lewis “questioned [Said’s] knowledge of history, philology, and Arabic” and criticized his “inflammatory tone” (New York Review of Books). Such fundamental gaps suggest serious deficits in Said’s scholarship, not mere stylistic flair.  
   - Marxist critic Aijaz Ahmad charges Said with “insufficient political discipline” and “self-aggrandizement,” accusing him of slavishly relying on European canons he otherwise decries (<quote>"a very conservative mind, essentially Tory in its structure.</quote>). If leading scholars find his methods inconsistent or ideologically driven, the works cannot be deemed reliably researched.

2. Inconsistent Methodology and Omissions
   - John Leonard observes that Culture and Imperialism is “exhausting in detail and maddening in its omissions, uneven in tone, overreaching and underargued” and that Said is “easily distracted” (<quote>"answering too many fire alarms, sometimes to pour on more petrol."</quote>). A well-researched book would maintain focus, present balanced evidence, and fill, rather than create, gaps.

3. Biographical Sleight-of-Hand
   - Said’s own memoir, Out of Place, is accused of deliberate misrepresentation of facts to construct a Palestinian identity, prompting Justus Reid Weiner to label the narrative “an elaborate sleight of hand” (<invalid_quote>“grow[ing] up not in Jerusalem but in Cairo… until his own departure”</invalid_quote> vs. Said’s claim). If Said’s autobiographical reliability is suspect, his analytical works on others’ texts inherit a credibility problem.

4. Vulnerability Invites Debate, Not Endorsement
   - The fact that Orientalism “remains open, vulnerable, provisional” is presented as a virtue only because it needs constant defense against well-reasoned attacks. Truly groundbreaking, well-researched scholarship withstands critique more robustly and does not require perpetual justification or revisions in light of basic factual challenges.

5. Political Motivations Undermine Objectivity
   - Said’s avowed “political intentions” and alignment with the PLO raise questions of bias. His “harsh critiques” serve an ideological aim of supporting the “oppressed” (postcolonial agenda), risking selective reading. Neutral scholarly research demands dispassionate evaluation of evidence, not ideological advocacy.

   - “Enlightening” is a subjective reaction. Enlightenment requires reliable foundations; Said’s acknowledged factual errors and selective use of sources invalidates putative illumination.  
   - Debater_B’s appeal to transformations in reading Aida or Heart of Darkness ignores that richer interpretations can arise from sound philological and historical research elsewhere; one need not accept flawed premises to appreciate texts.  
   - The volume of criticism—both left and right—should not be lauded as proof of value but seen as evidence of foundational weaknesses inviting attack.

Conclusion
   - The consistent, cross-ideological scholarly objections to Said’s research, his own autobiographical inconsistencies, methodological distractions, and ideological commitments cumulatively show that his works fail the standards of thorough, objective scholarship. They are insufficiently researched rather than reliably enlightening.

1. Praise for illumination and richness  
   a. The author states that Orientalism and Culture and Imperialism “fulfill the basic mandate of literary analysis, which is to illuminate the works they discuss.”  (quote “fulfill the basic mandate…” )  
      – If Said’s books did not truly enrich understanding, they would fail that mandate.  
   b. The author observes that after reading Said, “To return to Verdi’s Aida, Conrad’s Heart of Darkness… is to find them richer, stranger, and more complicated than you had ever imagined.”  (quote “richer, stranger…” )  
      – Enrichment of interpretation is the hallmark of enlightening scholarship.  

2. Enduring scholarly value despite controversy  
   a. The books are described as “permanent and exemplary works of late-20th-century criticism,” valued “in no small part because they invite so much argument” and “remain open, vulnerable, provisional.”  (quote “permanent and exemplary…” )  
      – Scholarship that endures invites ongoing debate; its provisional nature is a strength, not a weakness.  
   b. The very existence of formidable critics (e.g., Bernard Lewis, Aijaz Ahmad) attests to the impact and centrality of Said’s work in shaping post-colonial studies.  If the works were insubstantial or “not well-researched,” they would not sustain such high-profile scholarly engagement over decades.  

3. Author’s endorsement of intellectual methodology  
   a. The author praises Said’s “rigorous methodology” inherited from Harry Levin’s comparative approach and describes Beginnings as “painstakingly close formal analysis and displaying crushing erudition.”  (quote “crushing erudition” )  
      – Said’s approach in his foundational book demonstrates his capacity for meticulous research, undermining claims that his later work is untrustworthy.  
   b. The author emphasizes Said’s commitment to “placing ‘criticism over solidarity,’ speaking truth to power, and steering clear of gods that fail.”  (quote “criticism over solidarity” )  
      – This intellectual integrity suggests that Said’s scholarship strives for honesty and self-critique, not ideological sleight-of-hand.  

4. Rebuttal of “not well-researched” claim  
   a. Cherry-picking and omissions are normal in monumental syntheses: the author acknowledges the works are “exhausting in their detail” and “overreaching and underargued” in places but still “incendiary” and “exemplary.”  (quote “exhausting in their detail” and “incendiary… exemplary” )

      – If one accepts superficial allegations, one misses Said’s substantive arguments and the enriching insights his criticism provides.  
   c. The author’s own field (Commentary) once “flourished more widely” in an era of engaged criticism.  His praise of Said’s multifaceted career across literature, music, and politics shows broad respect from diverse intellectual communities.

He has assailed the corrupt, authoritarian regimes that rule most of the Arab world, punctured the ideological phantasms of Pan-Arabist nationalism and reactionary Islam alike, and bemoaned the impoverished state of Arab cultural and intellectual life.    - A work’s “permanence” in controversy is not proof of reliability but of persistent epistemic insecurity. If Said’s analyses were sound, critics would refine, not demolish, his premises. Instead, Bernard Lewis questions “knowledge of history, philology, and Arabic” and Aijaz Ahmad charges “insufficient political discipline” and “self-aggrandizement” (<quote>"a very conservative mind, essentially Tory i</quote>).

2. Methodological Inconsistency and Omissions
   - John Leonard admits Culture and Imperialism is “exhausting in its detail” yet “maddening in its omissions, uneven in tone, overreaching and underargued” and that Said is “easily distracted” (<quote>"answering too many fire alarms, sometimes to pour on more</quote>). Robust research anticipates counter-evidence and maintains coherent argumentation, not scattershot indictments.
   - Debater_B concedes “overreaching and underargued” passages. One cannot excuse systemic gaps in a sweeping work. Enlightenment requires completeness, not “gaps” to be filled by critics or readers.

3. Biographical Credibility Undermines Scholarly Trust
   - Said’s own memoir (<quote>Out of Place</quote>) faces charges of “elaborate sleight of hand” by Justus Reid Weiner, alleging misrepresentation of childhood (Cairo vs. Jerusalem) to “spin” his Palestinian identity. If Said fabricates or omits basic personal facts, his scholarly integrity is suspect. One cannot trust analyses rooted in potentially ideological self-mythologizing.

4. Political Agenda Threatens Objectivity
   - Said’s “political intentions” and role in PLO activities create a conflict of interest. His advocacy for a bi-national state and critique of Israel’s “continued expropriation” risk selective reading to serve “the oppressed” narrative (<invalid_quote>“post‐colonial agenda”</invalid_quote>). Neutral criticism requires dispassionate scrutiny, not polemical aims.
   - Debater_B’s appeal to “speaking truth to power” (<quote>"criticism over solidarity,</quote>) masks an ideological platform. Ideological commitments often lead to confirmation bias, as critics like Ahmad and Lewis demonstrate.

Rebuttal of “Enlightening” Claims

1. “Illumination” Based on Flawed Premises
   - Transformation of reading Aida or Heart of Darkness is moot if foundational premises (e.g., historical, linguistic context) are flawed. Enrichment built on unsound scholarship misleads rather than enlightens.
   - Other scholars offer rich interpretations without resorting to Said’s contested theories; enrichment can come from rigorously documented philological and historical studies.

   - No scholar praises a work’s “exemplary” status because it is “incendiary”—this signals a polemical device rather than stable knowledge (<invalid_quote>“incendiary… exemplary”</invalid_quote>). True exemplars become standard references, not perpetual battlefields.

3. “Crushing Erudition” in Beginnings Does Not Generalize
   - Said’s early work on Conrad reflects narrow literary analysis under Levin, not the vast historical, social, and linguistic scope of Orientalism. Success in one domain does not guarantee competence in another. Critics uniformly note his inadequate mastery when he ventures beyond literature into history and philology.

Taken together, cross-ideological scholarly objections to Said’s knowledge and methods, his own biographical dishonesty, methodological scattershotness, and ideological bias demonstrate that his most famous books fail to meet rigorous standards of research.
